Dew of Heaven
DYOO uv HEV-un
n. phr. (the dew as a figure of blessing given from above, and of humiliation)
Hebrew tal ha-shamayim — tal, dew or night mist, and shamayim, the heavens; in Daniel the Aramaic tal shemayya. Dew in Palestine falls without rain and was indispensable to the summer crops.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The blessing Isaac intended for Esau and gave to Jacob begins with it: “Therefore God give thee of the dew of heaven, and the fatness of the earth, and plenty of corn and wine.” The order is theological as well as agricultural. Dew is named before the fatness of the earth because in that land the summer brings no rain at all, and the night dew carried the crops through the dry months; it falls silently, without thunder or cloud, and cannot be stored, gathered, or compelled. It is therefore Scripture's natural figure for a blessing that is purely given — daily, quiet, and wholly outside man's management. Isaac's word to Esau keeps the phrase but reverses its position: “thy dwelling shall be the fatness of the earth, and of the dew of heaven from above”, and the sequel shows how differently the two blessings ran. Daniel turns the figure to humiliation. Nebuchadnezzar is told that he shall be driven from men, shall eat grass as oxen, and “they shall wet thee with the dew of heaven, and seven times shall pass over thee, till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will.” The same dew that blesses a covenant son soaks a proud king sleeping in the open. In both cases it comes down from heaven unbidden, and in both it teaches the same lesson about who gives.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Dew, the moisture collected from the atmosphere and deposited on the surface of the earth in the night. The dew of heaven, Genesis 27:28, a figure of blessing silently given from above.

Dew, the moisture deposited on the earth in the night season.

Hebrew tal, dew or night mist, indispensable to the summer crops.

God give thee of the dew of heaven, and the fatness of the earth, Genesis 27:28.

Thy dwelling shall be the fatness of the earth, Genesis 27:39, to Esau.

They shall wet thee with the dew of heaven, Daniel 4:25, of Nebuchadnezzar.

Key Scripture

Gen 27:28 — "Therefore God give thee of the dew of heaven, and the fatness of the earth, and plenty of corn and wine:"

Gen 27:39 — "And Isaac his father answered and said unto him, Behold, thy dwelling shall be the fatness of the earth, and of the dew of heaven from above;"

Dan 4:25 — "That they shall drive thee from men, and thy dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field, and they shall make thee to eat grass as oxen, and they shall wet thee with the dew of heaven, and seven times shall pass over thee, till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will."

Deu 33:13 — "And of Joseph he said, Blessed of the LORD be his land, for the precious things of heaven, for the dew, and for the deep that coucheth beneath,"

Modern Corruption

A figure for blessing that cannot be manufactured is read sentimentally, and the agricultural fact that gives it force — that the land lived on dew through a rainless summer — is unknown to most readers.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. It suffers instead from a distance that flattens it. Readers in temperate countries with regular rainfall hear dew as a decorative word for morning freshness, and the blessing of Genesis 27:28 sounds like poetry rather than survival. In the land of the Bible the summer is rainless for months together, and the heavy night dew is what carried the vine and the grain through it. That is why the dew stands first in the blessing, ahead of the fatness of the earth: it is the daily, invisible, uncompellable supply without which there is no harvest to be fat.

Recovering the fact recovers the doctrine. Dew cannot be irrigated, stored, or bargained for; it descends or it does not. Scripture uses it accordingly for the kind of blessing that is wholly of gift — God's favour, His teaching dropping as the dew, the brethren dwelling in unity like the dew of Hermon. The counterpart in Daniel 4 keeps it from sentimentality: the same silent descent that nourishes a covenant household soaks a humbled king until he learns that the most High rules in the kingdom of men. The principle to recover is that the quiet provisions are the critical ones, that a man lives by mercies he never arranged, and that the right response to dew is not admiration of the scenery but thanks to the One who sends it down.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tal, dew or night mist; shamayim, the heavens; the silent summer supply that cannot be stored or compelled.

Hebrew shamayim, the heavens, whence it descends.

Named first in Isaac's blessing, before the fatness of the earth.

Indispensable in a land whose summers bring no rain.
